# Hard-to-vary report: opening chapters of *The Time Machine*

## 1. The question, frozen

The excerpt answers several possible questions (why time is a fourth dimension; why the Eloi are childlike). The opening makes one central: this is a frame story built around a skeptical dinner party, so the question it works hardest to answer is **why the narrator and the guests come to believe the Time Traveller actually travelled through time, rather than performed a trick or told a tale.** Range: from the first demonstration (the vanishing model) through the second dinner and the start of his told story. Kind: forward — what produces belief in the room.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **P1** The four-dimensional-geometry argument (Ch. I)
- **P2** The witnessed vanishing of the model, staged with explicit "no trickery" framing and named observer positions
- **P3** The Psychologist's "presentation below the threshold" answer to the "why wasn't it visible earlier" objection
- **P4** The larger, unfinished machine shown in the laboratory
- **P5** The Time Traveller's physical state on return: dust, cut chin, bloodied bare feet, limp, ravenous hunger
- **P6** The skeptical chorus (Filby, Medical Man, Editor, Journalist) who voice doubt in the room
- **P7** The narrator's own avowals of reliable witnessing ("I am absolutely certain there was no trickery")
- **P8** The deferred, uninterrupted narration ("no interruptions... agreed")
- **P9** The explicit reminder of his earlier "ghost" trick, raising the trick-hypothesis by name

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Held by / note |
|---|---|---|
| P2 vanishing | **Held** | Job: explain why men who know him as a trickster don't just call it one. Remove it and only argument + his word remain — Filby explicitly says argument alone ("black is white") never convinces him. |
| P5 physical evidence | **Held** | Job: explain the shift from entertained doubt to real unease. Poke: had he returned merely tired but tidy, the room would not have gone silent as it does; the text leans on the wound and bare bloodied feet specifically. |
| P8 deferred narration | **Held** | Job: let the extraordinary later content land without being derailed the way Filby derails Ch. I. Swap for continuous interruption and the earlier pattern (objection → rebuttal → stalemate) would likely repeat. |
| P9 the "ghost" reminder | **Held** | Names the rival explanation the rest of the evidence has to beat; without it the trick-hypothesis is only implicit. |
| P1 geometry argument | **Loose** (for this job) | Swap it for any other plausible-sounding technobabble and the belief outcome is unchanged — Filby rejects it regardless. It does do a job, but a different one, outside this frozen question: signalling the Time Traveller as "clever" rather than a huckster (contrast with Filby, "a pork-butcher could understand Filby"). |
| P3 threshold explanation | **Held if** | Job: answer "wouldn't a machine going into the past have been visible all along?" It's held only if the group's trust in the Psychologist's authority is itself accepted — the text just asserts that trust ("Of course," said the Psychologist, and reassured us) rather than testing it. |
| P6 Blank/Dash/Chose (the unnamed extras at dinner 2) | **Idle** | Removable with no loss; only the Editor and Journalist, who get distinct lines of mockery, do a job. The "Silent Man" is closer to idle too, though he supplies one visual beat (pouring wine, startled). |
| P6 Editor/Journalist specifically | **Held** | Job: stage a real, still-unconvinced audience at the story's end, so the persuasion is shown as partial, not total. |
| P7 narrator's avowals | **Borrowed** | Rests on the Victorian first-person "reliable witness" convention (the ghost-story frame), not on anything demonstrated within this passage. Not tested here. |
| Names, the specific year, character nicknames | **Loose, and free** | Convention/taste, not offered as explained; correctly not dressed up as load-bearing. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had the room stayed skeptical (as it nearly does after Ch. II — "wait until tomorrow... the common sense of the morning"), would P2 alone have supported that too? Yes — the vanishing alone is compatible with either outcome. Only once P5 (bodily evidence) and P8 (uninterrupted telling) are added does the outcome tip toward credence. So P2 is necessary but not sufficient; the flip test correctly separates the load-bearing pair (P5+P8) from the merely necessary opening move (P2).
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** The narrator asserts early that no trick "could have been played upon us under these conditions" — this is itself unproven, and the rest of the account leans on that assertion rather than independently earning it. A skeptical reader can note the conclusion is partly declared at the outset.
- **Reverse/direction.** The account is told retrospectively by a narrator who already believes; he may be selecting confirming details (the dust, the wound) with the ending already known. The text gives no way to check this from the excerpt alone — a real loose thread.
- **Pull.** P1 (rational argument, meant to give scientific respectability) pulls against P6 (Filby flatly unmoved by that argument). The more weight the text puts on the geometry lecture, the more visibly it fails to convince — so the text quietly demotes P1 to color rather than load, which is consistent, but worth naming as a tension resolved rather than absent.
- **Catch-all.** P3 ("presentation below the threshold... diluted") could explain away almost any missing anomaly and comes with no stated gauge — nothing the group could check to see whether it is doing real work or just absorbing an awkward objection.
- **What the change list leaves out.** No one in the excerpt independently examines the vanishing (only an impulsive glance under the table), and no one tests whether the Time Traveller's dishevelment could be staged in minutes. The strongest rival (trick) is named repeatedly but never put to a real test within this excerpt.
- **Provenance.** P2, P5, P9 are *built* — placed with the persuasion problem itself in view, and they commit to something checkable (would the room react the same to a tidy return? the text implies not). P1 and P7 are closer to *asserted/borrowed* — genre furniture rather than something argued for here.

## 5. What would tighten it

Two moves: (a) have someone act on the trick-hypothesis directly — search the room, examine the machine's underside, time how fast a disguise could be staged — rather than only voicing suspicion; (b) give P3's threshold explanation a gauge, some observable check that would show whether it is genuinely explaining the earlier-invisibility problem or just absorbing it.

## 6. What this does not show

This says nothing about whether time travel is possible, whether Wells's four-dimension argument is sound, or the prose's literary merit. It only sorts which narrative devices are doing real persuasive work in this excerpt versus which are decoration or borrowed convention.

## 7. One next step

Read on to see whether the novel later gives P5's job (physical evidence) a stronger, independent form — e.g., an object brought back — which would be the natural escalation of what already carries the most weight here.
